The Prime Minister has virtually made no reference to the treaty, though he says we are bound by it, a statement which heretofore I have not seen attributed to him or to the government of which he is the head. If we are bound by the treaty we are interested in its terms, whether we ratify it or not. Its terms vitally affect us. Anything we are bound by vitally affects our Dominion, particularly if it c ncerns the issues of peace or war. As an introduction to what I have to say as respects the treaty itself, let me agree-if I understood my hon. friend correctly-with the aspirations of the Prime Minister as respects our position within the British Empire. I think he expressed what is a common attitude of mind of the entire Canadian people. I think he reflected what is really in the hearts of the Canadian nation, namely that we should pursue our destiny within the circumference of the Empire, as a self-governing Do-

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
minion, and that in doing so we should seek honourably to discharge our .part by an honourable co-operation with the other dominions and the motherland. This position Canada takes well knowing all that is involved therein. We take it first of all because it is in harmony with the traditions of our country, and with the heart's desire of our people. We take it secondlly because we believe it is for the good of the world that this destiny should be ours. We believe it makes for world peace, that the British commonwealth of nations should hold together, and should exert their united force towards such world policies as make for the peace of all; and we take it thirdly because we feel that along these lines Canada's ultimate ends are best served and Canada will gain at the present time as well as ultimately more than she can in any other way, that the burdens of nationhood will be lighter, and the rewards of nationhood will be greater than they can be by any other course we can pursue.
The alternatives the Prime Minister has suggested are the only alternatives, nor is there very much difference between them. If we swing into independence, we are really in the orbit of the great republic and subject to the will of that- republic, to a far greater degree than, perhaps, at the moment we care to contemplate. Let us then take it for granted that from all standpoints we want to stand within the orbit of the British Empire and to comply with those requirements involved in that relationship. If this is to be our position and our future, there are two pillars upon which the future can be erected. We must first of all insist, as we have always done, the insistence year by year becoming less necessary, on the full exercise of our full governing powers, on the most complete autonomy for this Dominion as respects matters which concern ourselves. We have never been slow in following this requirement. Parenthetically may I add, that never was there a time when anything in the nature of abbreviation or subtraction from those full autonomous powers was less in the minds of the people of the British Isles.
There is another corner stone, though, upon which this future must be built. This is the one referred to by the Prime Minister himself. There must necessarily be cooperation, and a cordial co-operation, for the common purposes of empire between all the parts thereof. We cannot build a future on the basis of autonomy alone. It is impracticable; it is not possible and. further, it does not savour of honour. We must necessarily adopt the principle of co-operation.
We must seek, by pooling our judgment, by review of facts and by common outlook upon the future, to gain common ground with the other Dominions and Great Britain as to what should be our general course in respect of foreign policy and of matters of common concern. We must approach this necessarily in a spirit of friendship and of confidence, we cannot approach it in a spirit of suspicion, distrust; if we do, we can never succeed. I do not think we have any reason for lack of confidence; I believe the past and particularly the recent past afford us every ground for the fullest and most ample mutual trust.
Assuming that these two are basic requirements, let me ask first of all: Have they been lived up to? Have we been true to them in relation to the Lausanne negotiations? Is this correspondence permeated by a spirit of co-operation, or. is there not rather emerging out of every letter, the spirit which says: "Go on, dio what you like; if you get into trouble, we will decide then what our course shall be?" We not only willingly, but apparently gladly stepped aside and let the British plenipotentiaries, or as the Prime Minister chooses to describe them to-day the representatives, of Great Britain take what line they liked. We received day by day communications informing us of all that was going on. We laid them to one side. We offered no presentation of view at all; we offered no assistance; we contributed not the least to directing the policy of the Empire upon lines that we considered honourable and safe. We simply stood aside and said': "Go on at your own risk; if you run into the marshes, you are there, we are not; if you run into fire, you are there, we are not; we are not involved in any degree." Is that a spirit of cooperation? As a consequence, where are we now? We have a treaty that is binding upon us; we have a treaty that is equally binding on every part of this Empire,-in the words of Mr. Keith, whom the Prime Minister quoted, in the negotiation of which treaty we have not had a single word to say, in the terms of which we have never had the least voice or breath. All of those obligations binding upon us, as the Prime Minister now admits, are framed aside from us and we have never ventured even to express our views.
The Prime Minister's speech is quite consistent with the theory that he does not think the terms of this treaty are of any importance to us at all, because those terms he has not even deigned to discuss. As I speak of these terms, I do so with the full sense of the re-ponsibility and full appreciation of the fact that one must tread ground of this kind ex-
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

ceedingly ' warily, because one necessarily is not in immediate and direct possession of all those facts and surrounding circumstances that give certainty to judgment; but subject to that consideration, I say that the policy involved in the treaty itself and especially in the Straits convention is, I think, a mistake and a policy from which it was the duty of this government to endeavour to avert the British plenipotentiaries. It was the duty of this government to see to it that they adopted such means of communication and in-temegotiation as were clearly open to them to present the viewpoint of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does the right hon.
gentleman think that Canada should signify its disapproval of the treaty?

No, I do not; I do not think we are in position now to do so. But the reason we are not in such a position is the fault of my right hon. friend, (Mr. Mackenzie King). What we should have done is this- we ought to have sought, as we did at the conference of 1921, to avert the British government from a line which affected interests peculiar to Canada and directing it along a line which more suited Great Britain as a world Empire.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The treaty is not yet ratified. My right hon. friend has plenty of time.

I have told my right hon. friend that we are not in a position to complain of the treaty now, and the reason that we are not in such a position is the fault of himself. The reason the treaty is as it is, in some degree at least, is the fault of himself.
In what respect, may I ask?

I am just coming to that.
I do not think, generally, Great Britain is well advised to pursue a policy of European commitments ; Great Britain is not distinctly a European country-and there, unconsciously,
I refer to Great Britain, as a "country", meaning the whole Empire, just as those authorities do to whom the Prime Minister referred. Often in speaking of this Empire as distinct from another country, we refer to it as "this country." We do that in Canada and they do it in Great Britain. I do not think the British Empire pursues a wise course in launching upon European commitments, and I think this statement is all the more supportable to-day, more so than it would have been two, three or more years ago. Great Britain, [Mr. Meighpn.)
as I was saying, is not distinctly a European country. It is true she is within the orbit of Europe; but Great Britain is a world Empire, She bestrides the seven seas of the globe. At all points of her vast domain she has interests sensitive and peculiar, interests that may be involved sooner or later in commitments which she is making quite unconsciously and in good faith and which appear to affect the Empire only in Europe.
What does the hon. member mean by the word "unconsciously" in this connection?

I mean unconsciously
in this sense that, without the viewpoint of the outer dominions being presented, she is not aware how they are particularly affected by these commitments; she does not see the objections to these commitments as clearly as the dominions naturally would. Can I illustrate the point better than by referring to the negotiations of some two and a half years ago on the subject of the Anglo-Japanese alliance? The natural, indeed the primary, attitude of the British government was most decidedly in favour of a renewal of the alliance. The public correspondence and the proceedings clearly disclose this fact. And British policy was so directed, wholly in good faith, wholly in the belief that thereby Great Britain could best serve the interests of the Empire as a whole. This Dominion took a different view, and did so, certainly not because of any superior experience, nor because of any superior mentality on the part of its representatives; it was merely because we, living here in the western hemisphere, saw more clearly and intimately certain dangers that would ensue from such a policy. We understood better the great republic to the south and its attitude of mind towards the alliance; we understood why it looked askance at that alliance; we better understood their point of view than could any other portion of the Empire without our assistance. Therefore Canada presented her viewpoint and insisted upon it; and her viewpoint so impressed itself on the British representatives and the representatives of the other dominions that the whole line of policy was diverted; and what would have been in my judgment a dangerous line was abandoned in favour of one leading more certainly to peace. I refer to this matter only by way of illustration. I believe that in order that Great Britain''s position as a world power may be appreciated, and that 6he may most wisely determine her general lines of policy,

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
the dominions of the Empire owe it to her to present their viewpoints on all subjects that concern the issues of peace and war.
A treaty is now binding on us or will be shortly-I fancy it is now binding on us- under which Great Britain enters into certain special engagements as respects the demilitarized zone of the Straits, certain special engagements which may involve her in conflict with great nations to the East and possibly indeed with great nations further away. Those engagements she has entered into for a purpose which to her mind is thoroughly justifiable, because I have not the least doubt she believes they are the lesser price, by paying which she better avoids conflict than by adopting any other course. But having regard to her responsibilities the world over, and having regard to our peculiar position and the position of the dominions as a whole,-having regard, in a word, to the fact that Great Britain is not nearly so much a European nation as a world power, the course she has pursued is in my judgment not wise.
In venturing these opinions I said that I wanted to do so cautiously and subject to reservation, all the circumstances not being before me. But those circumstances should have been before this government; this government should have made itself aware of the whole environment, the whole of the relative facts, and should have been in a position to advise the British government aright. I make these statements also in full appreciation of the tremendous achievements of the British plenipotentiaries at Lausanne. I have some knowledge of the difficulties which surrounded them; I know that they were pressed and torn by all sorts of conflicting forces; I know that they confronted a Turkey drunk with the wine of military success, a wholly different Turkey from that which faced Britain at Sevres. I know that Lord Curzon and Sir John Rumbold had around them about as mountainous and insuperable obstacles as ever surrounded plenipotentiaries in any negotiations. And if it had been essential to secure the main purposes of the treaty, possibly it would have been wise then to have made these special European commitments. But looking at the matter from this distance it would appear to me that these commitments were not the price of other things of greater value obtained, other securities for peace which were deemed essential. If they were, then I would say, very well; we will have to stand by them. They looked rather to be something which were peculiarly the objective of Great Britain. I am inclined to believe that this was something which could have been 186
surrendered without affecting substantially the greater objects of the treaty itself. I say therefore that it was our business to have taken the very best means which it was within our power to adopt to make known the viewpoint of this Dominion in this respect. We should have taken every means of seeking to divert British policy from any course which we felt, having regard to our peculiar circumstances, might lead to danger.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For purposes of information, will my right hon. friend say what means should have been adopted?

There were a good many means, but this government's state of mind was to keep outside of all means, to keep outside of the circle. It was not the intention of the government to sit in with our other negotiators and representatives, not to. make known even to those who finally were decided on as Empire representatives the attitude of Canada towards any feature of the treaty at all.

Will the leader of
the opposition suggest that the government should not have acceded 11 the request of the British government and should have declined to send any special representative?
I will come to that in a moment; but for the present I say emphatically in reply to the hon. member, no.

What attitude
did the other dominions take, if Canada took none?

The matter has been so handled that we know nothing about it. But Canada is the leading dominion. Canada takes the lead in these matters; she did so at Versailles in all the negotiations leading up to the treaty.

Had Canada made such representations to Great Britain as would substantially have altered the terms of the treaty, had they been acceded to, and had those representations not been accepted by the British plenipotentiaries, would Canada still be bound by the terms of the treaty?

Just as she is bound today. Let us understand once for all that while we are within the Empire we mu* be bound by the terms of high political treaties. There is no way in the world of avoiding it; and the consequences of trying to avoid it would be far worse for us than the consequences of cheerfully assuming it. I thought it was established, and established at great price, that Canada has gained the right-a

Supply-Lausanne Treaty

right now cheerfully conceded for years-to have a say in all these negotiations, and to have some word in the direction of the policy under which the British Empire seeks to secure herself and to attain world peace.
The first we hear of these negotiations is by the letter dated October 27, 1922. That letter extended no invitation to Canada to send representatives to Lausanne; it merely stated that invitations had gone out the day before at the instance of Great Britain, Italy and France, to certain powers asking them to Lausanne to negotiate the terms of a treaty to end the war with Turkey, and to certain other powers asking them to Lausanne in respect to certain less distinctly important relationships-I refer to the United States and to Russia. Now, the Prime Minister seems to think that if it was intended that we should have anything to say in regard to the treaty there should have been an invitation to Canada right then to have separate representation at Lausanne-that those three powers should have sent out invitations to us. And because they did not he said in effect:	"All
right, you go ahead; we are outside now watching, we have nothing to say, but if you make a mistake beware of the consequences so far as Canada is concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not think my right hon. friend is quite accurately stating the matter. Before any invitations were sent by any one part of the British Empire in conjunction with other countries, I think that the dominions should have been consulted and asked whether they wished to be associated with the invitations.

I do not know what
occurred before, consequently I am not making any criticism of what happened prior to the letter of October 27. What I say is that Canada has never been invited to negotiations of this kind. Canada was not invited to Paris by the inviting powers; France sent the invitations to the various powers. Canada was not invited to Washington by the inviting powers; those invitations were sent by the President of the United States to Great Britain and to the other powers.
What about the Genoa conference?

I know what my hon.
friend has in his mind, but it does not appertain to treaty-making at all. Canada nevertheless was separately represented at Paris and at Washington; Canada was separately represented on the British delegation which represented the entire Empire there. Consequently
[Mr. Meighen.l
the time for Canada to have spoken was when this notification came from Great Britain advising us that these invitations had gone forth. True, Great Britain suggested- and I do not defend the suggestion, I think it was dn error, a very natural error which has been made many a time before-Great Britain suggested that we should be content with the personnel of the British representation. That was the meaning of the suggestion contained in the letter of October 27.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was not.
It was not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was no
suggestion at all. There was a positive statement as to the reasons why we could not be invited. My right hon. friend knows that.

That is in the other
letter. There were reasons given there why there should be only two plenipotentiaries and why Canada should not have distinct representation'-reasons which I cannot divulge, and which the Prime Minister has not divulged, but reasons which were given before and which were surmounted before. But what should have been the reply of the Canadian government when the communication of October 27 came? The reply should have been:	It is for us to say whether we are
interested in this treaty or not; we were interested in the war which makes the treaty a necessity, and we are interested in the conditions now which are to tell for peace or war in the days to come; we have just as much interest in peace as we had in war. But, if we could not be at the conference table -what reason was there why we could not have been in closest touch with the British representatives from the beginning? What reason was there why we should not have been there to advise the British representatives of the view point of Canada? We knew right well that whatever those British representatives did they did as representatives of this Empire. Does the Prime Minister mean to say that they did not sign that treaty as representatives of the Empire? They certainly did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They signed as representatives of Great Britain.

I have the treaty. It
is not made between Great Britain and all these other countries, it is made between " The British Empire " and all these other countries. I do not know that anything more is necessary to make clear not only that we are bound, but that the signatures appearing there are signatures representing the Empire,

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
which is a party to the treaty. Not only is the treaty of Peace so made, but all of those which might be called the subsidiary treaties contained in the blue book which embraces the treaty, are made between " The British Empire " and the Other countries, and the signatures there are necessarily on behalf of the country which is stated in the whole preamble and headline of the treaty and in its contractual part to be the country that is negotiating and signing. So, this government knew-that the men who signed the treaty were signing it on behalf of the Empire. The government knows and admits, that it binds the Dominion of Canada and every other part of the Empire.

The word "bind" has been
used very frequently in the course of this debate. May I ask the right hon. gentleman to define just exactly what that means? For example, would it mean that the treaty binds Canada to enter into war without the consent of this parliament?

It binds us just as it
binds Great Britain. The treaty does bind the whole of the British Empire to preserve that demilitarized zone. I would much prefer that it did not, and I do not believe it ever would have bound us if the will of Canada had been properly represented and pressed; but it does bind us to do that, and it binds us to take the consequences that may follow such action.

Suppose Canada had
gone to this conference and made her views emphatic, but that those views had not been accepted, what would the hon. member say as to our responsibility in that event?

Canada might have secured this result-I do not know that it would have been any very great achievement-we might have had a clause inserted, whidh frequently was inserted in treaties before, that it did not bind any dominion unless that dominion expressly ratified it.
Is not that the position now?

Not one whit. It binds
us just the same as every treaty in the days of our colonial history bound us. That is the position which this government has led us into, precisely the position we were in thirty years ago, when we were bound by every treaty although we had no say in it at all. The whole achievement of the ad-186*
ministration is to take the lead not in progress but in retrogression, to lead us back exactly where we were in our colonial days.

The right hon. gentleman
stated, and quite correctly, that the treaty is between the British government and the other contracting powers. But I should like to draw his attention to article 18 providing for eventualities in case the demilitarized zone is imperilled, where he will notice that the special reference is to Great Britain alone. Has my right hon. friend considered the question as to whether Canada is bound there?

I had not observed that, but I accept the statement of the Prime Minister, which in this respect is right: we are bound, in the words of Mr. Keith, in international law just the same as the rest of the Empire, and the same as Great Britain herself. I do not think the wording there would make any difference, for the reason that the treaty itself is between those contracting powers.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The words my right hon., friend mentions are in a separate convention known as the Straits convention.

Yes, I know that, but
the separate Straits convention is also mad* between the British Empire and the other contracting powers; consequently the British Empire is bound, just as the binding is accepted by the government this afternoon.
May I ask another question? Would the treaty be binding had it not been ratified by the parliament of Great Britain?

There is a sense in
which a treaty is binding before ratification, but the formal ratification must take effect before there is a final binding; that is true.

The point I want to make is this: if it is not binding until it is ratified by the parliament of Great Britain, then if we are co-equal with great Britain it is not binding upon Canada until it is ratified by the parliament of Canada.

Yes, but this government has acquiesced in a condition of affairs under which we are not co-equal at all. They have acquiesced, apparently cheerfully, in the old colonial situation. They have said: "We are quite content; you go ahead; you make a treaty in the name of the Empire. True, that binds us, they now admit but we are prepared to allow that to go on and have no say at all." Such was the manly attitude adopted
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

by this administration in the name of Canada! Now, am I not right? I appeal to the clear mind of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler):	I do not think he can take
the least exception to my statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes he can.

Well, he is more likely
to be master of his own mind than the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
knows that the power of ratification is in the king, not in the parliament either of Great Britain or of Canada. The parliament of Great Britain did not ratify the treaty, does not ratify it. Parliament merely approves of the ratification.

Very good; that is not
the point at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the point.

Not at all. I was not
on anything having the least relationship to that point. It is true that the act of ratification is the act of the high contracting power, His Majesty. The moving of His Majesty to act is by the government, and the government before moving gets the approval of parliament. But all this has nothing, to do with the point. The point is this, that we are bound to-day by the terms of a treaty in the negotiation of which, in the final terms of which, we have not had the slightest say. Now, what is our improvement over the position we were in long ago? I had not thought that all the advance made in these years was an advance for nothing. I thought it was an advance, first of all, in elevating the dignity of our Dominion; in putting us in a more consistent and self-respecting position; in providing that as we could not by any means escape responsibility in the event of a war, we should have something to say as to the direction of policy, as to whether that direction should lead to war or to peace. This is the advance that we achieved all through these years, but it has been thrown overboard by the present government and we are back now to thirty or forty years ago; we are back to the position we were in before we were a confederation. There Is not a member of the government who can distinguish between our relationship at this hour to this treaty and the relationship which would have existed before we were even a confederation.
How is it that we had to wait until this afternoon for even an admission from a member of the government that we were bound by any term of the treaty at all? We were led to believe by the Prime Minister's speech of
(Mr. Meighen.]
April 2nd that we were not bound by any part of the treaty. I appeal to hon. members behind the government:	Did they not
come this afternoon, having listened to the Prime Minister on the second of April last, in the belief that we were bound by no part of the treaty or at least in the be>-lief that such was the position of the government? What the Prime Minister said on the second of April was that the treaty did not impose any obligations on Canada. Now we are asked to draw a distinction between the imposing of obligations and the binding. Is there a distinction? The Prime Minister seeks to draw this distinction; when you bind a country you only do it legally, but when you impose an obligation you put a moral obligation into it. If I got the Prime Minister's conclusion-I had almost said, argument, but there was no argument; on this point there was none-what the Prime Minister sought to say was this:	We are
bound now by the treaty, but we are not bound in the event of war to do anything. We are able to do something if we like, depending on what we consider our moral obligation to be. Because we stood outside and allowed British policy to proceed in matters concerning us, in matters concerning the very issues of peace and war; because we stood outside, now we axe free in the event of war resulting not to do anything if we choose, or to take such part as we like. I wonder when we were not so free? I wonder when the time ever wTas that hon. members of the government at least did not insist day in and day out that we were absolutely free? We are free; we are absolutely free to-day, Our decision depends only on our sense of obligation as to what we should do should war come about as a result of any treaty. Will the Minister of Justice say we are not free?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the first good word my right hon. friend has pronounced this afternoon.

Well, I pronounced it
many a time before-never pronounced anything to the contrary. It wholly depends, whether we sign or whether we do not, upon our sense of the moral obligation involved, upon our appreciation of what our duty is and what our interest is; and we are the judges in all events both of our duty and of our interest. This supposed achievement is nothing on earth; we are not one whit ahead, so far as our freedom is concerned, of where we were before. There is this difference

I concede it freely-when we sign a treaty we then express our approval and we are not in a position

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
subsequently to complain of its terms. We express our belief that they are the best terms we can get, the best line of policy under all the circumstances that we can agree upon. This follows from signature, and nothing else on earth follows from signature. We always decide whether we enter a war by our measurement of our obligation and by our measurement and appreciation of our duty. But no matter what we may think of the terms of a treaty, if the peril is great enough, n peril which if it involves Britain involves ourselves, then in our own interest, no matter what other considerations may surround us, we would participate. We are guided by the location of the conflict. We are guided by what is to be guarded thereby. We are guided by what other parts are able to do in the circumstances. We believe that within the realm of empire wTe avoid far more perils than we encounter. We believe that by co-operation with them and helping to direct their course we are more likely to make for world peace; that is why we stay within the Empire. We believe the burdens are lighter and the rewards are greater. But the obligations upon us are moral in all events. The (Obligation is an obligation decided by our own sense of moral responsibility and of our interest. So this government, for the sake of a mere shadow, has permitted misunderstanding and friction to arise. This government, for the sake of a mere shadow, has abandoned all that we have achieved over ten rather weary and bloody years.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

In opening what I said
this afternoon, in my comment on the merits of the treaty itself, I regretted that it included certain commitments in the way of certain guarantees applicable to European territory which I feared might ultimately emerge as dangerous. May I make a little further comment on that subject to avoid misunderstanding?
I gave the general reasons which applied against such a general course of policy, namely, those reasons which had particular application [DOT]to Britain as a world Empire rather than as a European power. It may be in the mind of some that these commitments are not new, that they have been made in the past, and indeed certain appeared in the peace treaties proper themselves. There were certain such commitments in the treaty of Versailles, not
many; there wras one commitment in the treat}' of Sevres of which this parliament and the Empire generally approved, a commitment of very great consequence, a commitment which preserved the neutrality of the same Straits. It was not the same as the present engagement. It at that time was essential, and if I could be persuaded that the present one was essential as a security for peace, I would express no word against it, but I want to call the attention of the committee to a very substantial difference between the circumstances which prevailed at the time of the treaty of Lausanne, and the circumstances which surrounded the plenipotentiaries at the treaty of Sevres. At Versailles, at Sevres, the whole lines of policy were agreed on early in the proceedings. The general limitations in respect of this feature and that, reparations, military engagements, the labour treaties, all in various compartments, and the lines of policy as to each were determined upon and agreed upon, and-and this is the point- they were all laid down upon the great basic assumption that the future of the world's peace was to rest on the secure foundation af a League of Nations of world-embracing scope. This at least was the fond aspiration of the British people. Consequently, the same care need not have been taken against any special European engagements, for the reason that if the hope of the British people and of the treating powers of that time were realized, then the sanction of a world-embracing league would be behind. However, in this hope, in this dream, we have been doomed to very severe disappointment.
We have a League of Nations, it is true. That League I do not disparage. That League I am anxious to support, and I hope that Canada will continue in its support, but it is not the League of Nations that we first believed it would be. Outside its scope now are three great powers, three powers of the first magnitude. I do not need to mention two, but I do mention the United States of America. While the United States of America stands outside, outside the League and outside all the sanctions that the League implies, any special commitment of this Empire has a different meaning altogether. Then it is much more incumbent upon us to see that we do not attach ourselves to any particular group at all, and do not bind ourselves to engagements in Europe which afterwards may lead us to this side or to that wholly independently of what the immediate circumstances of the time may be. This feature I will not dwell on further now; nor
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

have I anything very special to add to what I stated this afternoon.
The intervening time, though, has only added to my bewilderment as to what may have been in the back of the head of this government from beginning to end of this negotiation. I was astonished this afternoon to hear from the Prime Minister, although I was glad, because it removes one subject of controversy which would doubtless be very, very embarrassing in days to come-I was astonished to hear from him this afternoon that the government regards Canada as bound by the provisions of the treaty; Looking over the correspondence I am all the more astonished. Can it be believed that Canada was in this mind at the time this correspondence was indited? Surely the government was of a different mind altogether then. The correspondence is wholly inconsistent with the stand the government takes now, and the government's position now in this respect is right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It never
changed.
I know the Prime Minister will have to say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is true.

But certainly the
British people could not understand it on that hypothesis; not only the British government and the British Prime Minister, and the. leaders of the other parties, could not understand it on that hypothesis, but newspaper after newspaper could not; none of them could, and nobody in this country could.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They all attributed motives to us we never suggested.

It has been the puzzle
of commentators ever since. Let me read what the Prime Minister said in this House and see if it is consistent with the theory he now advances that we are bound by the provisions of the treaty. I will read the whole of the last paragraph of his speech on the 2nd of April, because I think this new decision has been born since the 2nd of April. It is of very recent birth. He says:
We take the position that, not having been invited to the Lausanne conference, not having been represented there, not having, for the reasons that I have mentioned, signed the treaty, the treaty does not impose obligations on Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister
stated this afternoon that it did impose

obligations on Canada. I know the distinction he is drawing now. He says that its provisions bind us, but in the event of trouble arising out of them later, then the obligation to execute or to protect the treaty is different. Is that not what he says now? If it is not, he does not say anything now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend will look at the dispatch of December 8, 1922, he will find the British government said:
Any treaty resulting from the Lausanne conference will of course replace the treaty of Sevres, and until it comes into force a state of war between the British Empire and Turkey will technically continue. Treaty must therefore be binding on the whole Empire when ratified.
We have never raised a question on that point. We have never taken the slightest exception to it. We recognize the legal obligation.

The Prime Minister
did not repudiate it and say, "We do not agree with you," but repeatedly in the correspondence he says, "The" extent to which Canada must be bound by this treaty must be determined by the parliament of Canada."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear.
And now he says we are wholly bound. How can the extent be determined by us if we are wholly bound?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I made a distinction there. There is a difference between the position of the British Empire in its relations to Turkey and other countries in the effect of this treaty upon them in bringing about a relation of peace, and the obligations that may arise within the Empire itself having regard to the manner in which the treaty has been negotiated.
Obligations as to what?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As to the provisions of the treaty with respect to obligations and otherwise.
Does the Prime Minister say we are not bound by the obligation of the Straits convention?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I say this parliament will determine just how far it wall recognize any obligations in the matter of the Straits convention, if it comes to a question as to which part of the Empire will see that these obligations are enforced.

That is precisely the interpretation I put upon the Prime Minister's conduct. I am not seeking to misstate his

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
case, I am seeking to state it properly. I have understood that the Prime Minister and the government took the ground that we were not bound by the obligations of the treaty. Now it is clear his position is this: In so far as the treaty is concerned, the whole Empire is bound. In international law we are all bound alike. But when it comes to a later time, when the necessity arises, if it should1 arise, of protecting the treaty against violation, or maintaining the securities which the treaty establishes then what we will do depends on the parliament of Canada. As to the latter, I have not the slightest doubt that what we will do will depend on the parliament of Canada, and it would equally depend on the parliament of Canada, even though we were represented in the negotiation and finally ratified.
But does anybody imagine that this was in the mind of the Prime Minister and the government at the time all the correspondence took place. Read into that correspondence any reference to such a distinction as this. Did the Prime Minister, in reply to the invitation of October 27, 1922, say to the government of Great Britain, "You have told us you are going to negotiate a treaty, and who the representatives are going to be. You have stated to us that when the ultimate time comes, if we succeed in getting a treaty for signature, we will ask you to sign, and you have also stated that you will ask us to ratify." Did the Prime Minister add "No, we are not of the treaty, we are not of the negotiations. We will be bound by i-ts provisions, as long as nothing arises out of it, but if trouble ever arises, if ever the necessity to protect the treaty arises, then the extent to which we will participate, if at all, must be decided by the parliament of Canada"?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will find in the very first dispatch that it is stated in these words:
We deem it advisable to avail ourselves of the earliest opportunity to inform His Majesty's government that in our opinion the extent to which Canada may be held to be bound by the proceedings of the conference or by the provisions of any treaty or other instrument arising out of the same is necessarily a matter for the parliament of Canada to decide, and that the rights and powers of our parliament in these particulars must not be held to be affected by implication or otherwise in virtue of the information with which our government may be supplied.
That is what is stated and that is precisely what he has not been stating this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is precisely what I said.

No. Will the Prime Minister permit me to proceed? This afternoon he said, "We are bound by the treaty only in event of it being necessary to take positive action to carry it out". Does the right of the parliament of Canada intervene? I wait for those who smile to answer me. Is that not precisely what he said? Is that consistent with this statement I have read?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Absolutely.
My hon. friend was not frank with the British government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I take exception fo my hon. friend's words. I have in my hand a communication sent by this government to the British government, saying we availed ourselves of the earliest opportunity of stating that we would recognize no obligations under any treaty that might be effected otherwise than what this parliament decided. My hon. friend has no right to put contrary words into my mouth.

I have not done so.
Does the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) think I have put contrary words into his mouth? If not, why does he applaud? I have not put a single contrary word into his mouth, and the Prime Minister knows it. He says in this first telegram:
The extent to which Canada may be held to be bound by the proceedings of the conference or by the provisions of any treaty or other instrument arising out of the same is necessarily a matter for the parliament of Canada to decide.
I know he said that. That is wholly different from saying that when the treaty is made we know that as part of the Empire we will be bound by it, but, we warn you that later if it is necessary to protect the treaty the extent to which we will participate, if at all, must be decided by the parliament of Canada. Now I do not need to appeal to intelligent men to see the very great, wide and vast distinction. The British government would have understood that. Does the Prime Minister suggest that in the telegram of the 25th of November which followed, he only had it in mind to warn the British government that though we would be bound by the treaty and its terms until the time came to enforce it, or the time came to take care of a danger that arose out of it, we would not be so bound to act until the parliament of Canada decided that we should.
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

Mr. MoMASTER:	Is not that pretty
clearly set out in the telegram of the 31st of October?

Not at all. I am speaking as well of the telegram of the 25th of November. He uses this language:
Our government has not expressed a desire to have any treaty with Turkey which may result from the conference, submitted to the Canadian parliament for approval, before His Majesty is advised to ratify it. Nor do we wish to be understood as preferred any such request. My message was intended to make clear that we had no exception to take to Canada not being invited to be represented at the conference, but inasmuch as we had been informed that we would be invited to sign a new treaty and any separate instrument regulating the status of the Straits, we wished to make it perfectly clear that in our opinion the extent to which Canada may be held to be bound by the proceedings of the conference or by the provisions of any treaty or other instrument arising out of the same, was necessarily a matter for the parliament of Canada to decide.
So far that is precisely what he had said before. But this statement and what 'he says to-day differ. What he says to-day is a full statement of the position, and what he said before is not, and for this reason I read what follows:
We deem it of the utmost importance that there should be no misunderstanding as to our position with respect to Canada's obligations in this and kindred matters. In our opinion parliament will desire, as respects the treaty with Turkey and any other instruments arising out of the Lausanne conference, to reserve to itself the right to decide upon the merits of the case what action on the part of the government is right and proper. In this connection we shall be pleased to have authority to place before parliament all the information with which we may be from time to time supplied.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We did not
get any of it and thej' would not give us any.
Any information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
As to the negotiations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
May I draw
my right hon. friend's attention to the concluding remarks of the telegram in reply:
I do not think that it would be possible to publish any of the telegrams now being sent to you concerning the proceedings at Lausanne seeing that they often contain records of confidential interviews and impressions and other material intended only for private information.

I am aware of that. The British government did not consent that this information should go to parliament. I agree with that, but information was sent to the Canadian government. My point is this: The Prime Minister here asks the British government, in order that parliament might be in a position to decide how far we might be bound

by this treaty, for permission to lay before parliament the information which the British government had undertaken to supply. What in the world would parliament want with the information except to enable parliament to decide what to do about the treaty? What was in the mind of the signer of that communication is as clear as day. The Prime Minister said:	Before we are bound by the
treaty, parliament must act. You ask us to ratify. You say that you will submit the treaty to us for ratification. You say that you will want us to sign. These things parliament must decide. Therefore we want to lay the facts before parliament. If it was for parliament to decide whether we should sign or not, it was logical that parliament should know the facts. Does anybody imagine that it was in the Prime Minister's mind, when he asked that the information be laid before parliament as received by the government, he was not asking for it so that parliament would know what to do about the signing and ratification of the treaty? Certainly that was in his mind. Imagine his suggesting now that what was really in his mind was this: Inasmuch as we have had nothing to do with negotiating the treaty, Canada not being represented, we will neither sign nor ratify it, for this reason and this alone; but afterwards if anything happens out of it, if there is any danger, any need for its protection, any cause for its enforcement, then parliament will want to know how the thing was brought about, and therefore I want to lay these communications before parliament. This position is absurd. What the Prime Minister had in mind was the necessity of being in a position to lay the information before parliament when parliament was called upon to decide whether Canada would be bound by the treaty or not.

Is it not the fact that whether we are represented or cot at any conference, the British authorities can sign a treaty or enact a law which can be made applicable to the whole British Empire? I do not think that can be gainsaid as a matter of constitutional law. Then, whether we are represented or not, we are bound by what is done. Therefore, the only way in which we can get out of it is by resenting what the British authorities have done, and if they will not accept our protest, the only way is by rebellion or otherwise.

I do not think the hon. member is very far out. The British authorities, in making a treaty, especially in signing a treaty in connection with a war in which we took a part, can bind the rest of the Empire.

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
The hoe., member is quite correct in that regard, and this afternoon when he was putting those questions to the Prime Minister after much of the comment the Prime Minister had made, questions that indicated that we were really in colonial status now, I thought he indicated a pretty fair appreciation of the position,. That is exactly where we are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We have never been out of it.

We have been out of it. We have had the right of a self-governing dominion until now, but the Prime Minister not only abandbned that position but cheerfully abandoned it. He said. You did not ask us and we do not find any fault with you at all. He acquiesced in the most cheerful manner in the position which reduces us to the colonial status again.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Let me direct my right hon. friend's attention to this wording:
In our opinion parliament will desire, as respects the treaty with Turkey and any other instruments arising out of the Lauzanne conference to reserve to itself the right to decide upon the merits of the case what action on the part of the people of Canada is right and proper.
"Upon the merits of the case" refers to any further instrument which may arise in which reference may be made to the Lauzanne treaty with Turkey and parliament reserves the right to decide what action is right and proper under the circumstances. That is what those words were intended to mean and that is what they do mean.

I was just going to argue upon those words myself. If they mean that, then they have misled not only every commentator that I have read, but myself. I took them to mean, and the British government evidently took them to mean, that parliament would decide on the merits of the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: What nonsense!

If the Prime Minister
meant:	You have not invited us to the
conference and therefore we shall not sign and we shall not ratify the treaty, why did he not say so in his first message?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I said quite
as much. I said everything that meant that.
Nobody took it to mean that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, they did
and there was no mistake. I appeal to my
right, hon. friend; I made the statement at the Imperial conference, that this government did not intend to concur in the ratification of the treaty. That statement was never questioned there. It was never misunderstood excepting by those who wished to have it misunderstood.

I can not dispute that
the Prime Minister made the statement. I have no means of disputing it. I believe he did, because he says he did. That is included, however, in the secret report of the conference. The Prime Minister, if he took that position at the conference, should have seen that it was included in the record. He should not have left the record in such shape that that statement was in the secret report. Besides there is no indication or hint of it. in the correspondence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had not the
shaping of the record.

The Imperial conference met long after these communications were sent out. If the Prime Minister intended not to ratify and to base his refusal to sign or ratify the treaty, not upon the merits of the treaty, but upon the mere fact that we were not represented. then he should have said so in his first communication without any equivocation at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He did.

He did not. He said:
"No. you go ahead and make your treaty and we will decide on the merits of the case what to do about it. The parliament of Canada will have to act and to decide before we are bound by the treaty." The Prime Minister should have said, if he had the mind he has this afternoon: "You have not invited us to the conference, and because you have not, we are out of the picture; you go ahead; you will get no signature, no ratification." This would have been understood. Nobody understood such a thing from the Prime Minister's dispatches, and now after months of disputing, misunderstanding, schisms between the two governments, the Prime Minister says that he has found two university professors who can define where Canada is at to-day.

I was going to suggest
that the interpretation given in somewhat colloquial language by the right hon. member seems to interpret pretty well the first telegram of October 31.

That was a notification
that we would not sign, would not ratify the treaty?
Supply-Lausanne Treaty
Yes.

Nobody in the world
took it up in that way, and nobody after all the discussion has taken it up in that way yet. After all these communications, I would not take it up in that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That settles it.

I am in agreement with every other commentator I have ever read. The Prime Minister cannot name me one who has taken it up differently from myself. The Prime Minister should at least have been frank with the British government and said: If you do not invite us to the conference, we shall not sign and we shall not ratify." The right position however for him to have taken was to represent to the British government that we had vital interests in the treaty with Turkey. We had interests in the war and we had consequently interests in the treaty which was to close the war. But the Prime Minister did not even tell them he did not intend to ratify the treaty. He led them to believe that it was going to be for parliament to decide whether or not we should ratify the treaty. In that statement I put myself in the judgment of hon. members of every party in this House. I say, the Prime Minister led the British government to believe that it would depend upon the will of this parliament how far we should ratify the treaty or be bound thereby.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He did not.
They evidently believed that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not so, although my right hon. friend may give it as his opinion if he wishes to.
I give it as their opinion and mine and the opinion of any one who looks into the matter. Why were the British government misled? Did they deliberately mislead themselves?
I hope not.

No one across the floor
apparently knows yet why they were misled.
I know there are men now who know what our position is, or claim they do; but any one who has a clear interpretation of all the correspondence that passed on the subject will take the ground that the matter of ratification and the whole matter of being bound by the treaty was represented by the Prime Minister to depend upon the will of the parliament of Canada. I have stated that the right course for us to have followed was to have 
declared our interest in the matter and our right to be represented, at least on the British delegation, and our right to present our views. And in my judgment we could have obtained that right to representation there, even though there could1 have been only two sitting at the conference table. At all events we should have asked for that right and led the other dominions in the request; and in my opinion if we had done so we could have succeeded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The treaty is
not yet ratified. If my right hon. friend thinks that this parliament ought now to approve of it and be bound by all the obligations involved in it, he has only to move that we be so bound, and let us debate the matter.

I have answered that
two or three times, and I do not know what relevancy it has to the point I am discussing unless the purpose is to divert me from that point. I have already stated what should have been done. Imagine any one but the government of Canada moving in the House to ratify a treaty! We cannot take exception to-day to the terms of the treaty. Does the Prime Minister take exception to the treaty or to any of its terms? He says now that because we have not ratified it we are in a better position. But I have shown the House that when we do not sign a treaty, when we have nothing in the world to do with it and no opportunity of influencing the framing of it, we may be in a position to take exception to its terms afterwards, if event arises, and to complain of its policy. This is the only difference, and1 there is no other. And if this is worth gaining at the expense we have gone to, of a reversion to our old colonial status, all well and good. But such is not the judgment of the people of Canada; and anyway we have not gained even that. We are not in a position to-day to complain of the terms of the treaty. Does any one think we are? Does the Prime Minister say that we are in a position to complain of any single sentence or any obligation of the treaty?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Most certainly.
Mr. .MEIGHEN: W^e are?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.
Did the Prime Minister complain of the terms of the treaty at the Imperial conference?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have taken the position from the beginning that we were not present at the conference; those who

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
extended the invitations thought we were not interested as it was not a matter that concerned us.

I know the Prime Minister has difficulty in answering the question. But what I asked him was-and if he feels he cannot answer it because of secrecy at the conference, then it is a misfortune but it is his own fault-what I asked him was whether he had taken exception to any of the terms of the treaty as being unwise or on any other ground. Did he take exception at the Imperial conference when the treaty was fully explained and all the circumstances of its negotiation were revealed? Did he take exception to the terms of the treaty or did he not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I took the
position that this parliament would not approve of the treaty; I do not know in what more emphatic way I could have stated the position of this country.

Surely the Prime Minister does not press that statement. Did he state at the conference what was wrong with the treaty? Did he point to any feature of the treaty, as I have done this afternoon, and say, "This does not receive my approbation"? Did he refer to any specific sentence or clause of the treaty and object to it? He will not say he did; I am fully convinced that he did not. And if he did he should have seen that his objection was noted in the records to the public.

Does not the leader of the opposition see that the Prime Minister, having taken the view that, not having been invited to the negotiations we were therefore not called upon to express an opinion, he would have been unwise in offering one?

Not in the least. We had an opportunity to express an opinion all through the negotiations. Our government was supplied with all the information; I have never heard that it was complained of as being incomplete; I have seen repeated statements of British ministers to the effect that information was given daily. So that we were certainly supplied with the information and we knew the tendency of policy; we knew what was contemplated and we had a right to interpose an objection then. We did not do so; we sat by in a sort of sullenness and said nothing.
Oh, no.

Perhaps not sullenness,
but lonely, questioning isolation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Taking no
exception.

Certainly-taking no exception, when we should have taken it. We should have contributed our part to the terms of a peace for which our men died. Does any one suggest that we had no interest in the terms of peace-a peace that concluded a war in which many of our own men had fallen? Certainly we had an interest in the terms of peace. We have an interest in the terms of every treaty which sets out the security for the future peace of the Empire and of the world. But the Prime Minister took no exception, he offered no objection at all to the course pursued or the intention manifested by the British government; he sat at the Imperial conference and heard the terms of the treaty; in fact, he had had them before him three months prior to the time he attended the conference. Yet he took n'-exception to any one of the terms of the treaty. All he objected' to, as stated for the first time this afternoon, was the fact that we were not invited to participate in negotiating the terms of the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I stated the
position to this country.

In other words, so
long as we are not invited to participate we have no interest at all and no comment to make on the terms of a treaty affecting our future happiness. Now, Mr. Speaker, our future happiness and peace depend upon the rightness and the soundness of the terms of that treaty, as upon the rightness and the soundness of the terms of other treaties. Are we not interested in the peace securities stipulated in that treaty? Were we not interested in the treaty of Paris? Were we not interested in the securities obtained at Washington? Of course we were. And we are interested in this treaty, perhaps not in an equal but in a like degree; and never will this country submit to having to sit outside when terms are negotiated concluding a war in which we have participated and fixing the securities on which the peace of the future is to rest. Therefore I say that this supposed gain that we have achieved- if any one can imagine that we have the right to complain if trouble afterwards arises as to the terms of the treaty-this supposed phantom is gone, because the time at which we could have complained with advantage is past, and the government can offer no objection now. This government therefore has hot, been frank with the British administration nor with the people of Canada; it did not
(

take in the correspondence the position it now assumes; it did not make its course clear, unequivocal and unmistakable. Consequently we have landed now in the position where after a series of months of disputation we find ourselves bound by a treaty in which we took no part at all, we find ourselves bound by the provisions of a treaty in the negotiation of which we had nothing more to do than had Chile; we find ourselves, in a word, back to the status of the old colonial days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, oh.
My hon. friend is laughing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I will explain the reason later.

We are back in the old
rank, and that by the admissions that were made this afternoon. There is not a whit of difference between the obligations we are under now and those we would have been under by a treaty negotiated by Great Britain fifty or seventy-five years ago.

I do not want to be
interrupting my right hon. friend for he knows more about this subject than I do- but when were we ever under the colonial status?

When we did not have
a part and say in the negotiation of British treaties, in the determination of the foreign policy of the Empire.

But we are still bound
by British treaties with other countries whether we are represented in the negotiations or not, exactly as we were a hundred years ago.
Very good; but we had gained the right to be represented, and we ought to be represented.
Whether we are represented or not we are still bound.

We ought to take advantage of what we have secured. All this the present government has abandoned. That is what I complain of. From this afternoon on, the people of Canada will have some very serious thoughts as to the direction towards which this government is tending. If we want friction this is the course to pursue. If we are looking for future difficulties this is just the line to follow: Do not ask for any representation. Hastily acquiesce in the suggestion-in the stipulation, if you will have it that way-that we do not have representations on British delegations. Cheerfully 
step aside and say: We will not have a word to utter about the policy at all, but when the time comes that any difficulty arises out of the policy which you are pursuing, then we will decide whether we will take any part or not as one of the self-governing dominions of the Empire. This is just the policy which will lead to friction, if it is friction we are looking for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend mean to say that if to-morrow a difficulty arose between Great Britain and Greece or Roumania or Jugo-Slavia we ought of necessity to get into that difficulty at once?
The Prime Minister does not imagine that I mean anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, he does.

No, we do not want to
get into any difficulty.
Hear, hear.

We do not want to be
in any difficulty whatsoever. But you do not get out of difficulty by keeping your eyes blind to what is going on, you db not get out of difficulty by permitting Empire policy to pursue a line which is ultimately bound to involve us, you do not get out of difficulty by remaining heedless of whether such policy involves us or not. In matters that we are concerned with let us present our view, and let our view every time be dictated by the interests of peace, and of peace alone. This government has abandoned the whole undertaking, this government has abandoned all responsibility, this government has abandoned its duty to the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks which I shall make will be along the line of trying to realize in some way just what the position of Canada is at the present time. Regarding the invitations to the Lausanne conference, it seems perfectly plain from the correspondence that has been placed upon the Table, copies of which members have now in their hands, that the Canadian government was not invited to attend, but they were to be kept informed of the negotiations from time to time. That the treaty binds the whole Empire seemed to be made perfectly plain from the correspondence and from the arguments which we have listened to to-day. Canada was not represented by Canadian delegates, and therefore the Prime Minister has stated that the treaty will not be submitted to this parliament for ratification.

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
The leader of the opposition takes the ground that although Great Britain may have made mistakes at the conference, yet if the government had stated Canada's point, of view mistakes might be obviated in the future. Of that statement I have no criticism to make. However, we must remember that consultation means responsibility. I shall not attempt to define exactly what is the responsibility of Canada in regard to the Empire, but one thing does seem to emerge from all the discussion which has taken place-that when the King has signed a treaty it is binding upon the whole Empire.
We hear a great deal about secret diplomacy, and I am rather surprised at this late date to learn that so many things take place which cannot be revealed to members of parliament or to the country. It seems to me that we would be in a better position to deal with this matter to-day if we knew exactly what took place at the Imperial conference and at the Imperial Economic conference. In relation to secret diplomacy, I had handed to me to-day a statement made by Richard Cobden seventy-three years ago, and with the permission of the committee I will read it. I hope hon. members will realize just how fast we are travelling towards open diplomacy. This is his statement:
My own opinion is that we are on the eve of a revolution in the diplomatic world; that the old regime of mystification and innuendo and intrigue cannot survive the growth of the democratic principle:	that
diplomacy must be a public and responsible organization; and nobly again has Kossuth-
-the Polish patriot-
-assailed the stronghold of this spirit. What could be better than when he said: "Diplomacy tells us that the dinner is prepared and eaten and we (the people) have nothing to do but digest the consequences."
That seems pretty much along the line of some engagements that are entered into by individuals and govemm'enlts-they are all done in secret, but the people have to bear the consequences. I am inclined to believe, Mr. Chairman, that the less we have of secret diplomacy the better will it be for the country and for the world at large.
I have listened very attentively to the speeches of the Prime Minister and the right hon. leader of the opposition, but I am bound to confess that I do not yet know exactly what the position of Canada is in the British Empire. But that is what we are trying to define. It seems to me, however, to be one of the most difficult things to define. The Prime Minister of Great Britain, Mr. Ramsay MacDonald, also seems to be in a similar difficulty, for I notice he is thinking of calling a conference of delegates from the dominions to meet representatives of Great Britain in an effort to see if they cannot formulate some policy which will be common to the Empire and involve common action. I should really like to know just what the opinion of Prime Minister MacDonald is in respect to the relationship of the dominions to the British Empire.
Will my hon. friend permit me a question?
Oh, oh.

I have put questions to the right hon. Prime Minister and the right hon. leader of the opposition, and have been treated very courteously by both. Does my hon. friend's reading of the history of our status as a portion of the British Empire incline him to any other view than that we .stand exactly as we did seventy-five years ago, save that the British government accord us the courtesy of asking us to attend Imperial conferences? Is there any other difference?
Yes.
I cannot see it, and no person can show it to me as a matter of constitutional law.
What is the use of asking the question then?
I am asking to be shown the difference. My hon. friend puts himself forward as the supreme arbiter in all things.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

It is not to be expected that I should attempt to answer that question when constitutional lawyers have been addressing the House on it for the whole afternoon and have not yet clearly defined it. But I do not agree with the hon. member when he says we have made no progress; I think we have made a great deal of progress in the past seventy-five years. Nor do I agree with the statement made by the right hon. leader of the opposition that we have lost all that we had gained during the last ten years. We did not gain that position through diplomacy, although that may have had something to do with the action that the Canadian government have taken during past years. But that is not the reason, I say, why we have attained our present position. Canada has attained the position she occupies to-day through the gallantry of her sons on the fields of Belgium and France and through
