the large sacrifices which Canada has made. Canada has attained the position she occupies to-day because of her standing in the economic world and the general influence she exercises among nations. Her very material position, if no other, gives her a standing that she had not attained ten years ago, and we cannot, we will not go back to the position we occupied in the days previous to the war.

Will my hon. friend
permit me again? Will he kindly tell me where as a matter of constitutional law our position is any different from what it was fifty years ago?

There are some facts that
we cannot exactly define. Perhaps before this debate is over it will have dawned upon the minds of hon. members exactly what the position of Canada is within the Empire, but I cannot define it in so many words. Of this I am satisfied, however, that we have made' tremendous advancement during recent years toward national status. The Prime Minister stated, either to-day or on a previous occasion, that our part was to keep our commitments and obligations and be ready to throw ourselves into the scale of peace and act in the interests of the welfare of the Empire. I do not know that a sentence of that kind contains any definite meaning. It may be very useful; it may be a very good policy for us to pursue. At the same time it does not in any way begin to lead us out of the trouble we are in with regard to a definition of our position as a nation within the Empire. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made the statement

I think it was during the South African war-that Canada reserved the right to act or not to act, and when. That is about the position we occupy to-day. I am concerned as to what Canadian national status is really going to be in the future. As a rule, individuals and nations are fond of talking about their privileges and their rights. If Canada is to enjoy the privileges of a nation, to reach the status of independence even as a nation within the Empire, that status will also carry with it responsibilites. If we are willing to take the status of a nation, then we must be willing to assume the responsibilities of a nation. I question very much whether we have arrived at that stage, and I question very much whether we are in a position to attain it at this time.
The question of Imperial defence has not been brought up in this debate, and it is one which I am not inclined to undertake to discuss. It is much too difficult a question; it is one to which I cannot offer any solution. 
But one thought that comes into my mind is this: Does Canada as a com-9 pan. ponent part of the British Empire run any more risk from invasion than she would do if she were an independent nation? I do not think anyone in this House will accuse me of being other than British in sentiment. In fact I am inclined to believe that our very relationship with the British Empire involves a certain amount of danger from invasion in time of war. As regards the signing of treaties, when Canada has a particular interest in the matters concerned, when the treaty affects only Canadian interests, there will be no trouble in having the treaty signed by Canadian plenipotentiaries and brought into effect by the signature of His Majesty the King. I do not believe for one moment, notwithstanding the argument of the right hon. leader of the opposition that we are going to go back to the status we occupied ten, fifteen or twenty years ago.
I would like very much to be able to define the position that Canada ought to occupy. I cannot think of any phrase that will better express my ideas than a line of Tennyson's, that we go on "from precedent to precedent." The right hon. leader of the opposition finds fault with the government because he thinks we have perhaps let one precedent slip by that we might have taken advantage of. However, I do not think any irreparable damage has been done. I do not conscientiously believe that, the relative positions of Great Britain and Canada are any different to-day from what they were twelve months ago. Canada is in the position today of emerging from what might be called a status of irresponsibility to that of a free nation. I think you will find the same thing apply in many phases of life. For instance, there is a time when an animal emerges from the condition in which it is unable to look after itself and is about to reach that of independence. We seem to be just in that transitory stage. We are not a nation; we are not a colony; we are something more than a colony and a little less than a nation. That is about as nearly as I can define our position. I rejoiced this afternoon to hear the Prime Minister and the right hon. leader of the opposition say that they would prefer that Canada should go on in its development toward the status of a free nation inside the bounds of the British Empire. Perhaps I feel a little more strongly on this question than some other members of the House. I am Canadian through and through. My

children are native bom Canadians; I have no other interest except what is in Canada. But, Mr. Chairman, I can never forget the land that gave me birth. To me it is not only a matter of how Canada will grow in stature as a nation; it is a matter also of sentiment. I sincerely hope that whatever the future	may bring, Canada

It can only be for the advantage of Canada and of the whole Empire that we should have a league of British nations making for peace and for the welfare of the world. While having a warm affection for those little inslands on the other side of the Atlantic ocean, I would wish that Canada might ever remain at peace with the great nation to the south of us. It is unthinkable; you cannot imagine such an occurrence as war between Canada and the United States. I know that I have added nothing to this debate, but as I have said, it is most difficult to define our position. I have faith in the future; I have faith in the perseverance and the ability and industry and intelligence of the Canadian people; I have faith in the fair-mindedness and justice of the British government. Waterloo (Mr. Euler) while my right hon. friend was speaking. The power of ratification varies in different countries. After a treaty has been negotiated and signed by the representatives of the countries concerned, it has to be ratified by some part of the sovereign power in each country. In some countries the power of ratification is in the popular chamber, as in Portugal, for instance. In other countries it is in the second chamber, as in the United Startes. In Great Britain the power of ratification is in the Crown, and my right hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he read the first words of Lord Cur-zon's speech on moving in the House of Lords the bill concerning this treaty, read his statement that this treaty does not need ratification by parliament. The same thing was stated in the British House of Commons by Mr. Lloyd George respecting the Peace treaty after the conference art, Versailles, and it was stated in the Canadian parliament at the same time. Ratification by His Majesty the King makes the treaty valid and binding. His Majesty the King is the King of Canada, Australia, of New Zealand, as well as of Great Britain, and when he signs a treaty which declares peace with Turkey, all the nations of which he is king are at peace with Turkey, just as when he declares war, all the nations of which he is king are at war. This cannot be contradicted in any respect.
So, Mr. Chairman, ratification by His Majesty the King will make the treaty valid for all parts of the Empire, but as has been stated this afternoon and again to-night, parliament will always be the only authority to decide to what extent and the manner in which any obligation resulting from the treaty will be lived up to. It is for parliament to declare and decide-I think what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said this afternoon will be accepted by everybody in this House-what the extent and limit of those obligations shall be. The manner in which they shall be fulfilled may depend in large measure upon the manner in which they were assumed. In connection with a treaty to the negotiations and deliberations leading to the signature of which we were no party, a treaty with which we had nothing to do, surely the moral obligation is not the same as that resulting from a treaty in which we participated to the fullest extent. Last September the British cabinet, or, more accurately stated (as has since transpired), a section of it, apparently determined to run the risk of war with Turkey. We are not here discussing the merits or demerits of the policy itself, but we point out that neither the British House of Commons nor the Dominion legislatures were given any opportunity of debating the subject, nor were they given any data to enable them to judge of the circumstances which had led to so grave a decision. Now, that is not so with regard to our domestic affairs* After perhaps a good deal of disagreement and sometimes considerable conflict we have at last achieved national status so far as our domestic affairs are concerned, with some few possible minor exceptions; we have complete command over our own domestic affaire. But who will suggest that we have complete control over our foreign affairs? I think it is time that our attitude as to foreign relations should be clarified as far as it is possible for the government or for parliament to do so. We should declare and define our exact position in that regard just as we car. with the greatest simplicity and ease declare and define our position with regard to our domestic affairs.
As pointed out by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) there was a resolution of the Imperial War conference in 1917 pointing to the necessity of a constitutional conference for the purpose of trying to enlighten us on our relationships within the Empire. It was thought advisable that that conference should mot proceed during the course of the war and it was suggested that the matter
should be taken up at the earliest possible date after the conclusion of hostilities. The first Imperial conference after the war was held in 1921, at which the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) was present. Bitt for some unknown reason that constitutional conference was not proceeded with. In the proceedings of the 1921 Imperial conference we find this unanimous resolution-I read only a part of it:
Having regard to the constitutional developments since 1917, no advantage is to be gained by holding a constitutional conference.
As Sir Robert Borden, in his work already referred to, has said:
If the self-governing dominions may not have adequate voice and influence in the direction of the Empire's foreign policy, it is not improbable that some of them wll eventually have distinctive foreign polices of their own, and that may mean separation.
The situation is that we have not been able so far to arrive at any definition through consultation or through the avenue of a constitutional conference, so it seems to me that failing that we must set about ourselves to ascertain, if we can, exactly our position and exactly our responsibilities.
May I be permitted for a few moments to deal with the matter somewhat historically? During the period of our colonial status, in the earlier days of our history, there could be no question that we were not
10 p.m. entitled to any part in foreign policy and that we were under no obligation whatever to assume any burden in respect of foreign wars. I am not going to take the time to discuss with the members of the House the purposes or the ideas in the minds of the rulers of the Mother Country with regard to her colonies in those days when we enjoyed colonial status. But it is abundantly clear that Canada-and it is not to the discredit of England at all-was in those days looked upon as a place for commercial exploitation in the interests of the Mother Country. We must judge the age and the conditions which existed in that time, and during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries there can be no doubt that colonies were looked upon as I have stated. Let me read from a work The American Revolution recently published by a distinguished Oxford professor. He says:
To each generation belongs its modes of belief; and to the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries it was impossible to conceive of colonies which did not directly minister to the Mother Country's wealth.
Then the author quotes as an example the attitude assumed by one Martin Bladen, a member of the Board of Trade in England, * gentleman to whom belongs the rather ques-
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

tionable distinction of having been the first to propose the stamp tax for America. I may add that a member of the Board of Trade occupied a position in those days of even more importance than it is to-day. Here is what he says:
Every act of a dependent provincial government ought therefore to terminate in the advantage of the mother state unto whom it owes its being and protection in all its valuable privileges. Hence it follows that all advantageous projects or commercial gains in any colony which are truly prejudicial to and inconsistent with the interests of the mother state must be understood to be illegal and the practice of them unwarrantable, because they contradict the end for which the colony had a being and are incompatible with the terms on which the people claim both privilege and protection. For such is the end of colonies, and if this use cannot be made of them it will be much better for the state to be without them.
May I then refer those who are interested to the dispatch sent immediately after the treaty of Peace of 1763 by Lord Egremont, one of the secretaries of state, to the Lords of the Board of Trade, requiring them to report on this question:
By what regulation, the most extensive commercial advantage may be derived from these cessions, and
How these advantages may be rendered more permanent and secure to His Majesty's trading subjects.
In part, the Lords of the Board of Trade, reported on the 8th of June, 1763:
The most obvious advantage arising from the cessions made by the Definitive treaty are: the exclusive fishery of the river St. Lawrence, on all the coasts of the gulf of St. Lawrence, and the islands in that gulf.
And it goes on to indicate how advantage may be taken of the fishery and the fur trade. Similarly, the purposes for which the colonies *were held were indicated in 1791 in a dispatch written by the English secretary for the Colonies to Lord Dorchester. This question was asked:
-^by what means, the connection and dependence of Canada, on this country may be so preserved and cultivated, as to be rendered most beneficial to Great Britain during its continuance, and most permanent in its duration.
With the advent of free trade in England in the forties of the nineteenth century this idea that a colony was intended for exploitation by the Mother Country happily vanished. This new view synchronized with the granting of responsible government to the colonies, a condition which was not only accentuated but was reinforced by the federation pact of 1867.
With regard to military affairs so far as the relationship between the Mother Country and the colonies was concerned, it is interesting to find that Earl Grey, the Colonial Secretary, from 1846 to 1852, in evidence given before a

royal commission in the Old Country in 1861, used these words:
I think that the very notion of a colonial relation between this country and our colonial possessions implies protection on our side and obedience on the other, within certain bounds.
Then we find that in the Hamilton-Godley military report of the 24th of January, 1880, these words are used:
Thirdly, we dissent from the argument founded on joint interest. If England was considered bound to contribute to the defence of her colonies merely because she is interested in their defence, it might fairly be argued that the obligation is reciprocal, and that the colonies, being deeply interested in the safety of England, ought to contribute systematically and habitually towards the defence of London and Portsmouth. But the ground on which we hold that England is bound to contribute towards the defence of her colonies is, that the Imperial government has the control of peace and war, and is therefore in honor and duty called upon to assist them in providing against the consequences of its policy.
This is a very clear intimation that when the relationship of colonial status exists the Mother Country is under obligation to provide any necessary protection, because she is the one who is responsible for the condition of peace or war.
Coming later to the military position in 1902 at the Imperial conference of that year the War Office presented a memorandum of which I quote a part:
Prior to the outbreak of the war in South Africa, as far as any general scheme for the defence of the Empire as a whole had been considered, it was assumed that the military responsibilities of our great selfgoverning colonies were limited to local defence, and that the entire burden of furnishing reinforcements to any portion of the Empire against which a hostile attack in force might be directed fell on the regular army. There may possibly have been some pious hope that in time of need the colonies might rally to the Mother Country, but no definite arrangements were made, nor were inquiries even on foot as to whether such aid might be expected, and if so, in what strength. Indeed, the necessity for it was by no means realized and its reliability was doubted.
I have made these quotations for the purpose of indicating the position, of the colonies with respect to the Mother Country according to the responsible views of leaders in the Mother Country itself. Now let me survey the Canadian attitude for
10 p.m. a few moments. We fought in two British wars in Canada, the American Revolutionary war, and the war of 1812-1814. Neither of these wars was of course, of our own making. Our next experience was in 1861. An effort was made in that year by the Duke of Newcastle to have Canada prepare for the possibility of hostilities with the United States in connection with the so-called Trent affair. The Colonial Secretary, the Duke of Newcastle, undertook to exercise

Supply-Lausanne Treaty
pressure on the Canadian government with reference to military preparation. Parliament declined to pass the required legislation and the Duke of Newcastle on the 22nd of August, 1862, expressed his regret. He urged the resumption of efforts by the Governor General in that direction and indicated very clearly what ought to be done. He suggested military co-operation under the direction of the Adjutant General, and gave various other suggestions. Now I direct the attention of hon. members to the reply of the Macdonald government of that day, because I think the reply clearly indicates the position of Canada, even at that early day, with regard to taking part in wars the making of which we were not a party. I am quoting from the reply of the Canadian government:
The dispatch of His Grace involves matters of the highest importance and affirms a principle which for the first time comes in a practical shape before the people of Canada. Your Excellency's advisers have not been unmindful of the discussions upon the subject which have taken place in the Imperial parliament, but until now they have not been called upon to consider the principles of a policy so gravely affecting the relations of Canada to the Mother Country .... It is not doubted that the same mutual regard and confidence will be exhibited in any communication or negotiation which may follow His Grace's dispatch. At the same time, however, it is felt that in dealing with a question affecting so deeply the present and future welfare of the province, care should be taken to base any arrangements that may be entered into upon something more solid than sentiment, more enduring than any proposal not recognizing the rights and interests of the Canadian people.
After arguing in favour of the voluntary system as against the compulsory system, the memorandum goes on as follows:
The people of Canada, doing nothing to produce a rupture with the United States, and having no knowledge of any intention on the part of Her Majesty's government to pursue a policy from which so dire a calamity would proceed, are unwilling to impose upon themselves extraordinary burthens. They feel that, should war occur, it will be produced by no act of theirs, and they have no inclination to do anything that may seem to foreshadow, perhaps to provoke, a state of things which would be disastrous to every interest of the province. On this ground their representatives in parliament assembled rejected the proposition to organize 50,000 men, or, indeed to commit the province to a much smaller force; and recent elections in various localities embracing more than a third of the population of the province, have shown that in this respect public feeling has undergone no change.
Proceeding further:
Another suggestion embraced in His Grace's dispatch is well calculated to excite surprise. Your Excellency's advisers allude to that portion of the dispatch in which His Grace proposes to remove the control of funds required for militia purposes from the domain of parliament. His Grace is evidently aware that the proposition wears the aspect of "an interference with the privileges of the representation
of the people," and it is certain that any measure liable to this construction never will be, and ought not to be, entertained by a people inheriting the freedom guaranteed by British institutions.
Then again:
Your Excellency's advisers now turn to the general argument which underlies the argument of His Grace. That the right of self-government has for a correlative duty the maintenance of provision for defence, is a proposition which in the abstract is indisputable in the case of governments of states which are sovereign in themselves. As between a colony and the parent state it cannot be said to exist in the same sense. A British colony must submit to all the consequences of conflicts produced by the policy which Her Majesty's government may carry out in the interest of the Empire at large. It is not enough that a colony endowed with self-government provides for the preservation of peace and order within its own boundaries. It is not enough that a colony so situated must endure all the consequences of a line of action which its own legislators have no voice in originating and towards the termination of which they can do nothing. A further responsibility is held to attach to the colonial relation. The colony, although the theatre of ruinous hostilities, must furnish its quota in aid of the Imperial army and contribute a share to the attendant expenditure.
The dispatch goes on 'and says the Canadian government cannot assume this responsibility. That is the first time this matter was drawn to our attention in Canada. The next time we were asked to participate in an overseas war was in 1885, in connection with the war in the Soudan and may I take the liberty of quoting the reply of Sir John A. Macdonald to the request for Canadian reinforcements? To Sir Charles Tupper, who was then High Commissioner in London, on the 12th of March, 1885, Sir John wrote these historic words:
I wrote you a hurried note the other day on this question, and have both before and since talked it over with my colleagues, and we think the time has not arrived, nor the ocasion, for our volunteering military aid to the Mother Country. We do not stand at all in the same position as Australasia. The Suez canal is nothing to us, and we do not ask England to quarrel with France or Germany for our sakes. The offer of these colonies is a good move on their part, and somewhat like Cavour's sending Sardinian troops to the Crimea. Why should we waste money and men in this wretched business? England is not at war, but merely helping the Khedive to put down an insurrection, and now that Gordon is gone, the motive of aiding in the rescue of our countrymen is gone with him. Our men and money would therefore be sacrificed to get Gladstone and Co. out of the hole they have plunged themselves into by their own imbecility. Again, the reciprocal aid to be given by the colonies and England should be a matter of treaty, deliberately entered into and settled on a permanent basis. The spasmodic offers of our militia colonels, anxious for excitement or notoriety, have roused unreasonable expectations in England, and are so far unfortunate. I daresay that a battalion or two of venturous spirits might be enlisted, but 7d a day will cool most men's warlike ardour.
I want to draw hon. members' attention particularly to Sir John A. Macdonald's
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

words in that dispatch when, he said that the reciprocal aid to be given by the colonies to England should be a matter of treaty deliberately entered into and settled on a permanent basis.
The next occasion on which we were involved in a war was during the Boer War, into which we voluntarily entered. I think we enlisted something like 8,000 men and spent something like $3,000,000 on that war, only to be met by the denunciation of Joseph Chamberlain at the Imperial Conference of 1902.
Before leaving to attend that conference Sir Wilfrid Laurier used these words in the House of Commons:
It would be the most suicidal policy that could be devised for Canada to enter into that vortex in which the nations of Europe, England included, are engaged at the present time.
On the 10th of October, 1910, speaking at Montreal, he used these words:
Does it follow that because we are exposed to attack we are going to take part in all the wars of the Empire? No, we shall expect to take part if we think proper.
Now one of the most important declarations of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's on this important matter was at the conference in 1911. Sir Joseph Ward had proposed a resolution there regretting that the colonies had not been consulted by the British government with reference to the Declaration of London. During the debate Sir Wilfrid used these words:
We may give advice if our advice is sought; but if your advice is sought, or if you tender it, I do not think that the United Kingdom can undertake to carry out that advice unless you are prepared to back that advice with all your strength and take part in the war and insist upon having the rules carried out according to the manner in which you think they should be carried out. We have taken the position in Canada that we do not think we are bound to take part in every war, and that our fleet may not be called upon in all cases, and, therefore, for my part, I think it is better under such circumstances to leave the negotiations of these regulations as to the way in which the war is carried on to the chief partner of the family, the one who has to bear the burden in part on some occasions and the whole burden on perhaps other occasions.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier saw with a very clear and discerning statesmanship that if he took part in the consultations of Empire, it necessarily meant that we must assume responsibility, but in all his actions and in all his efforts it is perfectly clear that he kept away from consideration of these questions involving advice, for the good reason that I have given that it meant the responsibility of this country.

We have been told on numerous occasions that as a result of that war, and as a result of the peace, that we have very definitely improved our position, that we have secured an improved status. I desire to read one or two statements of some gentlemen who ought to know so far as that particular matter is concerned. Lord Milner uses these words:
There is no kind of authority which in practice (whatever may be the theory of the constitution) the parliament and people of the United Kingdom claim any longer to exercise over the parliaments and peoples of the self-governing dominions. We have got to decentralize our conception of Empire, and realize that each member of the British commonwealth is equal in status to every other, and, from its own point of view, the centre of the whole.
Was that the time Lord Milner was Governor of South Africa?

No, that is at a comparatively recent date.

The common effort and sacrifice in the war inevitably led to the recognition of an equality of status between the responsible governments of the Empire. This equality has long been acknowledged in principle, and found its adequate expression in 1917 in the creation, or rather the coming into being of an Imperial war cabinet, as an instrument for evolving a common Imperial policy in the conduct of the war.
Sir Robert Borden, in a speech quoted in the official report of the war cabinet, said:
But we have always lacked the full status of nationhood, because you exercised here a so-called trusteeship, under which you undertook to deal with foreign relations on our behalf, and sometimes without consulting us very much. Well, that day has gone by.
Sir Robert Borden, referring to his attitude at the Peace conference, has said:
On behalf of my country, I stood firmly upon this solid ground; that in this, the greatest of all wars, in which the world's liberty, the world's justice, in short the world's future destiny were at stake, Canada has led the democracies of both the American continents. Her resolve has given inspiration, her sacrifices been conspicuous, her effort was unabated to the end. The same indomitable spirit which made her capable of that effort, and sacrifice, made her equally incapable of accepting at the Peace conference, in the League of Nations or elsewhere, a status inferior to that accorded to nations Jess advanced in their development, less amply endowed with wealth, resources and population, no more complete in their sovereignty, and far less conspicuous in their sacrifices.
In the treaty of Versailles dated 28th of June, 1919, provision was made by which under certain circumstances, it was arranged as follows:
Article (1) Provides adequate security and protection to France, Great Britain agrees to come immediately to her assistance in the event of any unprovoked movement of aggression against her being made by Germany.
But provision was made for a separation of obligations so far as the dominions were concerned in the following article:
Article (5) The present treaty shall impose no obligation upon any of the dominions of the British Empire unless and until it is approved by the parliament of the dominion concerned.
There we find a very clear separation of the obligations of the dominions as compared with the Mother Country. The British parliament approved of that provision, and consequently cannot now be heard to say that we are one and indivisible, and all necessarily bound by exactly the same foreign policy.
The next step in our position, perhaps not very important, was the Halibut treaty.
If the British authorities did that, and the Canadian authorities would not accept it, would that not be tantamount to a declaration of independence?

I do not think the failure to ratify the treaty or any reservation would necessarily be tantamount to a declaration of independence. I was about to suggest that the Halibut treaty would probably represent one stage. I do not place much importance upon it; but its importance, I think, comes particularly by reason of the fact that the king, acting as respects Canada, overrode the advice of the Colonial Secretary and gave a Canadian representative power to sign the Halibut treaty. It is of primary importance too in that it led to the series of resolutions to which the Prime Minister referred this afternoon, at the Imperial conference of 1923, resolutions which, I suggest, very clearly recognize a separation of obligations as between the various parts of the Empire.

If His Majesty the King gave that authority overruling the British authority, if the Governor General in Canada is a representative of His Majesty, why cannot the Governor General in Canada give the same scope of authority to Canadian ministers without reference to the British authorities if we are not still dependent upon the British authorities?

I do not know what might happen in certain eventualities, but there can be no question about this, that the king acts on the advice of either his British ministers or his Canadian ministers. In connection with the Halibut treaty, he acted on the advice of his Canadian ministers and appointed a Canadian plenipotentiary to conclude that particular treaty.

If we are not still dependent on the British authorities, why cannot the Governor General act on the advice of Canadian ministers without reference to British ministers at all and say we are independent without going around the bush?

There is much camouflage in connection with this question, I agree with my hon. friend. The fact remains that the king is king, not only of Great Britain, but of Canada, and he is the final authority as regards these treaties.
He has his representative here, though.

If what I have suggested in
outline means anything at all, it means two
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

or three very definite things: first of all, that Canada has never agreed in advance under any circumstances to participate in British wars. On the contrary she has consistently declined to be 'bound to participate without the action of her parliament. Again, there has been a clear separation of interests amongst the various parts of the king's dominions and that has been repeatedly recognized. There has also been recognized a separation of obligations with respect to foreign countries even in the matter of war. That has been not only recognized, but officially provided for.
That brings me to this particular treaty. There can be no doubt that in some treaties Canada has participated in the negotiations; she has been represented; she has secured the approval of this parliament, and she has invited the King's ratification; but in respect of the Lausanne treaty now before the House, Canada took no part in the negotiation of it ; she was not represented at the conference; she did not sign, and now the government, at the request of the British government, has refused to ask this parliament to give its approval to the ratification.

I thank the Prime Minister
for the correction, because I do not want to misstate his position.

Is my hon. friend's
whole argument not tantamount to this, that we are an absolutely independent nation; that the only thing we recognize is a human being overseas, the King of England, and we take his imprimatur as a matter of course? That seems to 'be his whole argument.

With some hesitation, I
agree to a limited extent with what my hon. friend has stated. I rather thought that was the position until I heard the discussion this afternoon, and I am frank to say that I am not just sure now what the position is.
I am in the same position.

In any event the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition both agree in this particular, that we are bound by this treaty. I do not agree with that view. If such is the fact why all this historic separation of obligation? Personally, I cannot see, if there is that equality of status of which I spoke a few moments ago, how one portion of the Empire which alone negotiates, which alone signs, which alone participates in the framing of that treaty, is thereby enabled to impose that treaty as a binding obligation upon any other portion of the self-governing dominions. Supposing the position were reversed; suppose Canada as part of the Empire happened to be at war with a country and alone made peace, I wonder if this rule would work the other way and if such a treaty of peace would be binding upon the Mother Country. I doubt that very much. The Prime Minister has spoken also about our being involved in some moral obligations. I cannot see the distinction. If we are bound, we are legally bound, and if we are -bound by the terms of this treaty, then it is our duty, as a country which honours its contracts to see that the treaty is carried out to the full, at least to the limit of our ability. It was claimed by the Prime Minister that <the treaty was made on behalf of Great Britain alone but in answer to that I need only say that, as pointed out by the leader of the opposition, the treaty on its face describes one of the contracting parties as the government of the British Empire, and I cannot therefore accept the mere statement of Lord Curzon in a debate as proof to the contrary.

*The governments of the British Empire, France and Italy, in agreement with the government of Japan, being desirous of finally re-establishing peace in the East, and having invited on the one hand Greece, Roumania, the Serb-Croat-Slovene state, and also the United States of America. .	.	.

In that treaty itself, I think the plenipotenti-

It is strange that Lord Curzon should have made this reservation with regard to this trade convention and ignored it so far as the more onerous provisions of this treaty are concerned. I shall speak for a moment now with regard to the final act in this matter, which is the ratification, or the act which converts this treaty from a treaty in escrow to an operative treaty, that transforms reality into fact. The ratification by the king is the final act which gives operation to the treaty of peace. The king is an international entity; he is the one who makes the treaty of peace. He acts on the advice of his responsible ministers and in this ratification it seems to me he is acting on the advice of his responsible ministers in Great Britain and not on the advice of his responsible ministers in Canada. In other words the king will undoubtedly ratify this treaty acting on behalf of his British ministers; but unless his ministers in Canada give their approval then I fail to see how the king can ratify on behalf of this country.

If the king ratifies on
the advice of the Imperial government that ratification applies to Canada, irrespective of whether our ministers agree or not. The hon. member cannot get away from that.

That is the question; but I
am not so sure that the King acting on the advice of his British ministers can perform the final act of ratification binding this country. It is not an unusual situation for the king
of one country who is also the king of another to find himself in different positions with respect to his separate kingdoms. For example, history shows that the Georges in England were also kings of Hanover; and many a time the King of England found himself in his capacity as King of Hanover at war with European nations although he was not at war in his capacity as King of England. And similarly it may well be that the King of Canada may not be at war when the King of England is at war.

Perhaps we had better
be independent.

I will suggest in a moment
what seems to me the logical position in this matter. Now, there are many other treaties.
I have in my hand a list of the treaties appearing in King's Monthly List of March-April, 1924; this list comprises about a dozen treaties. I wonder what interest Canada has in any of them? I wonder whether she has been consulted? I find one between the British government and some foreign power with regard to Spitsbergen, a treaty regulating the status of that country and conferring the sovereignty on Norway. I wonder what concern we have in that particular treaty. I find a treaty with Czecho-Slovakia, and some arrangements with Germany, with France and with Japan; and there is an important treaty with Nepal, providing for the importation of aims into that country. That is an important matter and I wonder whether the government of Canada was consulted regarding it; I wonder whether they gave their seal of approval to the ratification of that important treaty. One can see how absurd the situation would be if we had to be bound by every treaty which the British government should chance to ratify. Here is a country, the exact geographical situation of which I confess I do not know, for the importation of arms into which a treaty 'has been provided which may ultimately result in war. Surely no one would suggest that we as a country are bound hy any such treaty as that. To urge otherwise would be to reverse the historic policy of this country.
The Prime Minister has indicated that there are several courses we might pursue. We may, he said, be one commonwealth of nations. I do not like that term, I must frankly say; I do not understand the term if we are to be a nation with equal status. It seems to me that the logical position for Canada to assume, the goal towards which we must develop, is to obtain complete control not only of our domestic affairs but of our
Supply-Lausanne Treaty

foreign affairs as well; we must become really, in fact and dn law, an independent nation. Having achievied that status and in that position I for one at least would welcome a full and frank association with all the other dominions of the British Empire and with the British government itself in order that we might go on and achieve in this world a fuller destiny and make the Empire something which would be really and eminently worth while. That seems to me the sound logical basis on which we may make progress in the future. But if we leave our status in the nebulous, hazy state it rests at present trusting that somehow good will finally come of it, I am afraid that we are merely anticipating disaster.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to propose a resolution asking the concurrence of the House in the action which this government has taken in this matter. I think it is important that these matters should be presented to the House in some definite way so that the House may arrive at a conclusion and express that conclusion not only to the members of the British Empire but to the world at large. A discussion such as we are having will undoubtedly be quite beneficial; but it is not directed to any particular object, and we are sometimes apt-I know I am myself-*-to stray from the subject. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the only way which seems possible to me for the purpose of indicating the approval of this parliament of the action of the government, I beg to submit a resolution to the committee. I do not come to this conclusion by the same process of reasoning as the Prime Minister, but I do think that the action of the government in this matter has been the right one. I move therefore that this item be reduced by the sum of one dollar for the purpose of approving of the government's action in not submitting the document known as the Lausanne treaty to parliament for approval.
dhe CHAIRMAN:	This amendment as
submitted is not in order: It is not possible to give reasons in committee of Supply for a vote to be reduced, increased or varied in destination. As the amendment stands therefore I must rule it out of order.

I am not sure; Mr. Chairman, that your ruling will be received with anything like dismay on the part of the committee. The amendment is remarkable, but it is no more remarkable than the reasons which preceded it. I was frequently at a loss to know just what- my hon. friend was driving

at, but I got the purport of his observations in the few sentences before the close of his speech in which he advocated the independence of Canada. After we have secured that independence he is ready to co-operate to build up the Empire. I would prefer myself to build up the Empire before destroying it rather than after. I do not rise for the purpose of replying to the speech of the hon. member, for the simple reason that it was conceived in a spirit of criticism and an aversion to things Imperial which I do not share at all, and which, I think, are not shared by any portion of the House. Independence is a fine-sounding thing; but when hon. members with a sense of responsibility sit down to realize all that is involved in it I do not fancy there will be any very serious discussion on the subject either in parliament or in the country.
I do wish to make however a very brief reply to certain statements of the Minister of Justice. I comoliment him on the preservation of his wit and of that extraordinary command which he has attained of a language not his own.
I wish I could compliment him on the logic of his address in general. Suffice to say, as expressive of my estimate of his intellect, that I feel he has the same appreciation of that logic which I have myself. He made an attack upon a position which I took in relation to the Chanak negotiations of September 1922, and to the conduct of Canada in respect thereof-I had not said the stand of Canada, because Canada had no stand. Canada's position was more that of crouching impotence and indecision than any standing up position one way or the other. He depicts me as attacking the government and its position on that occasion, declares that I denounced1 what the government was doing and said what I thought Canada ought to do, to send a reply "Ready, aye ready." I did not denounce the government's position, because we did not know then what its position was. As a matter of fact it was some time afterwards before we knew that the government had no position, that they simply sheltered themselves behind some platitudes, in other words, crawled under the table and declined to express any view on the stand the British government was taking or as to the stand Canada ought to take.

speechtext:
There was a
certain communication sent by Mr. Churchill at the time asking if Canada was prepared to join with the British government in sending forces to the Near East.. Does my right hon. friend say that that was a communication sent with the knowledge of the British government?

I do not know what
is the point of this interruption. Do I say the British government's communication was sent by the British government?

speechtext:
I am referring
to the so-called dispatch sent out broadcast to the press, whether that was an authorized dispatch on the part of the British government?

Oh, the Prime Minister
is raising the point whether the member of the government who sent that dispatch had the authority of the other members to do so?

speechtext: Yes.
Oh,, I do not know what that, had to do with what I was saying.

I will come to it in a moment, but it had not the remotest relation to what 1 was saying. At the time I made the address referred to no reply had been sent by Canada at all.

Not at the time I spoke.
